report: Conclusion: the claim “soursop cures cancer in humans” is unsupported and should be treated as false. Soursop/graviola (*Annona muricata*) contains acetogenins that can kill cancer cells in lab and animal models, but major cancer centers say there is not enough reliable clinical evidence that it treats cancer in people, and it should not replace surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, immunotherapy, or other proven care (https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/treatment/complementary-alternative-therapies/individual-therapies/graviola; https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/graviola). Human research is still preliminary: a 2024 publication was only a protocol to test safety/tolerability of an *A. muricata* leaf product in advanced malignancy, not proof of benefit (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31659754/). Safety is also a concern: annonacin is toxic to dopaminergic neurons in experimental work and has been investigated in relation to atypical parkinsonism (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14521988/). Eating the fruit occasionally as food is different from taking concentrated leaf/seed extracts or capsules, which may carry neurotoxicity, blood-pressure, blood-sugar, and drug-interaction risks. Anyone with cancer should discuss supplements with their oncology team and avoid delaying evidence-based treatment.
